# gpt-oss-120b (GptOssForCausalLM, LLM) - MI300X Standalone Analysis

## Executive Summary

This capture covers a mixed steady-state vLLM inference window (3 prefill-decode steps, 29 decode steps, batch 510 / concurrency 62) on a single MI300X rank. The GPU is busy for only 1825.40 ms of the 27907.71 ms window, so 93.45% of the capture is device idle while compute accounts for 6.54%. Collective communication is entirely absent (0.00% exposed) and device copies are negligible (0.01%), so the idle time comes from the host dispatch path, not from communication or memory transfers. Within the compute time itself, the dominant cost is the unfused two-stage MoE expert path (1392.51 ms, 76.3% of compute), which splits each expert group into a separate up-projection (plus SwiGLU) and down-projection launch and round-trips the intermediate activations through HBM; that path carries both quantified compute findings below. The remaining categories — vendor GEMM, MoE routing-metadata helpers, and paged attention — are each under 7% of compute and run within expected bounds for tuned library kernels, so no per-kernel tuning opportunity in them clears the reporting threshold. The headline idle figure itself warrants care: 88.6% of all idle sits in 145 stalls that recur at a fixed every-256-kernel-completion cadence inside graph replay, a signature that tracks the measurement path rather than model structure, so it should be re-measured with reduced tracing before engineering effort is committed against it.

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Total Time | 27907.71 ms |
| Compute % | 6.54% |
| Idle % | 93.45% |
| Exposed Communication % | 0.00% |
| Top Bottleneck Category | GEMM (6.78%) |

![Performance Improvement](data:image/png;base64,)

---

## Compute Kernel Optimizations

Findings from per-category kernel analysis (GEMM, attention, MoE, elementwise, normalization, Triton, and miscellaneous operations).
Summaries of recommendations from the per-category sub-agents, focused on individual kernel efficiency.

### Top Operations

<!-- impact-begin kind=top_ops -->
| Rank | Category | Time (ms) | % of Compute Time | Ops |
|------|----------|-----------|-------------------|-----|
| 1 | GEMM | 123.675 | 6.78% | 17 | <!-- top-ops-row low=null high=null -->
| 2 | other | 102.117 | 5.59% | 45 | <!-- top-ops-row low=null high=null -->
| 3 | InferenceAttention | 101.83 | 5.58% | 8 | <!-- top-ops-row low=null high=null -->
<!-- impact-end -->

### 🔴 P1: Unfused MoE up-projection stage dominates expert path (Triton)

**Insight**: The MoE up-projection plus SwiGLU stage consumes 917.5 ms of GPU kernel time across 1152 launches and writes its intermediate activations back to memory before the down-projection stage reads them again.

**Action**: Replace the two-launch up-then-down expert path with a fused MoE expert kernel that keeps the post-activation intermediate on-chip across both projections. If no fused variant is available for this backend, profile the dominant up-projection kernels for tile-size and wave-occupancy tuning at the decode shape, where achieved throughput is far below the prefill shapes.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item category=moe_unfused low=0.48 mid=0.99 high=1.48 -->
**Impact**: impact_score: 0.99
<!-- impact-end -->
> **Warning — estimated:** No performance model for this op; impact is derived from its E2E GPU-time share (3.29%), not a gap projection.

→ *See [Detailed Analysis: Compute kernel insights > P1](#detailed-analysis-compute-p1) for details*

---

### 🟡 P2: Unfused MoE down-projection stage pays a second launch per expert group (Triton)

**Insight**: The MoE down-projection stage consumes 474.98 ms of GPU kernel time across 1152 separate launches that exist only because the expert path is not fused.

**Action**: Fold the down-projection into the same fused MoE expert kernel as the up-projection so the stage no longer requires its own launch or its own reload of the intermediate activations. If fusion is unavailable, tune the down-projection kernel independently, focusing on the decode shape where throughput is lowest.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item category=moe_unfused low=0.25 mid=0.51 high=0.77 -->
**Impact**: impact_score: 0.51
<!-- impact-end -->
> **Warning — estimated:** No performance model for this op; impact is derived from its E2E GPU-time share (1.7%), not a gap projection.

→ *See [Detailed Analysis: Compute kernel insights > P2](#detailed-analysis-compute-p2) for details*

---

## Kernel Fusion Opportunities (Experimental)

> **Note:** Kernel fusion analysis is experimental. impact_score projections estimate the recoverable fraction of E2E with 85% memory/compute pipeline overlap. Kernels without perf models use their measured trace time as-is. Candidates where fewer than 75% of kernels have perf models are not reported. Actual recoverable time depends on implementation feasibility and interaction effects.

No kernel fusion opportunities detected.

All 25 raw fusion candidates in this trace were rejected by the deterministic gate because they are container frames or already-fused compiler-generated paths (Inductor-compiled modules, vLLM Triton MoE kernel entry points, and `matmul_ogs` Triton matmul frames) rather than separable adjacent kernels. The MoE expert-path fusion opportunity is reported under Compute Kernel Optimizations above.

---

## System-Level Optimizations

> **Note:** System-level analysis is exploratory. The patterns and recommendations below are under active development and may be refined as system-level analysis matures.

Findings from system-level analysis (GPU utilization, memory transfer patterns,
communication/compute overlap). These affect the GPU pipeline as a whole.

### 🔴 P1: Re-measure idle with reduced tracing before acting on the 93% figure

**Insight**: 88.6% of all GPU idle time comes from 145 stalls averaging 159 ms that land at exactly every 256th kernel completion inside graph replay, a cadence tied to the measurement path rather than to any model structure.

**Action**: Re-capture the workload with kernel-level tracing disabled or sampled, or with a profiler buffer large enough to cover a full step, then re-derive the idle percentage from that capture before committing engineering effort to the headline 93% number.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item low=null mid=null high=null -->
**Impact**: Not quantifiable from trace data
<!-- impact-end -->

→ *See [Detailed Analysis: System-level insights > P1](#detailed-analysis-system-p1) for details*

---

### 🟡 P2: Extend graph capture to the non-graph execution path

**Insight**: Steps that replay a captured graph keep the device nearly back-to-back with a median inter-kernel gap under 10 us, while steps that dispatch operations one at a time from the host show a median gap of 681 us and leave the device idle for 77% of their wall time.

**Action**: Capture the mixed prefill-plus-decode shapes into graphs the same way the decode-only path already is, so those steps replay from a pre-recorded dispatch list instead of per-operation host calls. Where a shape cannot be captured, reduce the number of host-visible operations per step through fusion so fewer launches are needed.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item low=null mid=null high=null -->
**Impact**: Not quantifiable from trace data
<!-- impact-end -->

→ *See [Detailed Analysis: System-level insights > P2](#detailed-analysis-system-p2) for details*

---

### 🟢 P3: Repeated small host-to-device stagings in the per-step path

**Insight**: 70 host-to-device transfers of near-identical size (8.02 us average, 9.42 us maximum) recur across the window, which indicates per-step control or metadata tensors are being built on the host and pushed to the device each iteration rather than reused.

**Action**: Pre-allocate a pinned host staging buffer for these recurring tensors and issue the transfers asynchronously on a dedicated copy stream, or hoist values that do not change between steps into device-resident tensors. Expect the host-to-device transfer count to drop and the remaining transfers to stop serializing against the compute stream; total exposed memory-copy time should fall below its current 1.781 ms.

<!-- impact-begin kind=p_item low=null mid=null high=null -->
**Impact**: Not quantifiable from trace data
<!-- impact-end -->

→ *See [Detailed Analysis: System-level insights > P3](#detailed-analysis-system-p3) for details*

---

## Detailed Analysis

### Compute Kernel Insights

<a id="detailed-analysis-compute-p1"></a>
<!-- reasoning-candidate tier=compute rank=1 -->
#### 🔴 P1: Unfused MoE up-projection stage dominates expert path (Triton)

**Identification:** These operations were flagged because they account for a significant share of end-to-end GPU time but have no performance model, so no roofline efficiency could be computed for them. They run on a Triton backend inside the causal-language-model wrapper of the MoE model, launched from the Triton runtime through the compiled model graph. The kernel names show an MXFP4-weight matrix multiply with a fused SwiGLU activation, which identifies this as the first of two expert projection stages. Four distinct shape signatures were grouped: one small decode-sized batch invoked 1044 times, and three larger prefill-sized batches invoked 36 times each. (source: `moe_unfused_metrics.json` → `category_findings[].estimate_method` = `heuristic`, `operations[].efficiency.efficiency_percent` = null, `operations[].percent_of_total`, `operations[].library`, `operations[].module_chain`, `operations[].call_chain`)

**Data:**

| Operation |  Args  |            Kernel Path                  | Kernel Name | Time (ms) | %E2E | Count |FLOPS/Byte| Efficiency | Bound |
|-----------|--------|-----------------------------------------|-------------|-----------|------|-------|----------|------------|-------|
| pseudo_op::moe_triton_unfused_up (decode) | (64,3072) bf16<br>(64,128) bf16 | triton/runtime/jit.py(726): run | _matmul_ogs_NNT_bf16xbf16xmxfp4_32x256x128x1_swiglu.kd | 580.65 | 2.08 | 1044 | 9.19 | — | — |
| pseudo_op::moe_triton_unfused_up (prefill) | (7211,3072) bf16<br>(7211,128) bf16 | triton/runtime/jit.py(726): run | _matmul_ogs_NNT_bf16xbf16xmxfp4_64x256x128x1_swiglu.kd | 155.482 | 0.56 | 36 | 761.69 | — | — |
| pseudo_op::moe_triton_unfused_up (prefill) | (6188,3072) bf16<br>(6188,128) bf16 | triton/runtime/jit.py(726): run | _matmul_ogs_NNT_bf16xbf16xmxfp4_64x256x128x1_swiglu.kd | 136.233 | 0.49 | 36 | 668.33 | — | — |
| pseudo_op::moe_triton_unfused_up (prefill) | (1074,3072) bf16<br>(1074,128) bf16 | triton/runtime/jit.py(726): run | _matmul_ogs_NNT_bf16xbf16xmxfp4_64x256x128x1_swiglu.kd | 45.159 | 0.16 | 36 | 130.68 | — | — |

**Reasoning for Slowdown:** This stage matches the unfused multi-stage MoE pattern. Each expert group pays a separate kernel launch for the up-projection, and the post-activation intermediate tensor cannot stay on chip for the down-projection that follows. The decode-sized signature alone accounts for 580.65 ms over 1044 launches, which is 2.08% of end-to-end GPU time. That signature has an arithmetic intensity of 9.19 FLOPS/Byte and reaches only 17.49 TFLOPS/s and 1.9 TB/s, which is the low-arithmetic-intensity regime expected when a small token count is spread across many experts. The prefill-sized signatures sit at the opposite end, with arithmetic intensities of 130.68 to 761.69 FLOPS/Byte and 130.1 to 252.27 TFLOPS/s against a 708 TFLOPS matrix peak. TB/s, FLOPS/Byte, and efficiency for MoE are uniform-routing approximations, because the byte estimate assumes tokens are distributed evenly across experts. Cannot assess expert load balance from trace data. Cannot assess routing quality from trace data. Cannot assess token distribution from trace data. No roofline efficiency is available for these operations, so the remaining gap cannot be attributed to a specific hardware limit from the trace alone.

**Resolution:** A fused MoE expert kernel removes the intermediate write-back between the up-projection and the down-projection, so the post-SwiGLU activations never round-trip through HBM. That cuts the bytes moved per expert group and removes one kernel launch per group, which matters most for the decode signature where 1044 launches each move very little work. Precision narrowing is not an option here because the expert weights are already MXFP4, the narrowest practical precision. If no fused variant exists for this backend, the remaining lever is per-stage kernel tuning. Bottleneck identified — generate reproducer for kernel team.

**Impact estimate:**
<!-- impact-begin kind=detail_estimate low=0.48 high=1.48 -->
- Low end impact_score: 0.48
- High end impact_score: 1.48
<!-- impact-end -->

<a id="detailed-analysis-compute-p2"></a>
<!-- reasoning-candidate tier=compute rank=2 -->
#### 🟡 P2: Unfused MoE down-projection stage pays a second launch per expert group (Triton)

### System-Level Insights

<a id="detailed-analysis-system-p1"></a>
<!-- reasoning-candidate tier=system rank=1 -->
#### 🔴 P1: Periodic 159 ms device stalls dominate idle and track the measurement path

**Identification:** Idle time was flagged because the device is unoccupied for 93.45% of the capture window. Breaking that idle into individual gaps shows it is not spread evenly. 145 gaps of 50 ms or longer carry 88.6% of the total idle time, and the remaining roughly 35000 gaps carry the rest. Replaying the same captured graph 29 times produces the same five long stalls every time, at kernel positions 8, 264, 520, 776 and 1032 within the step. Those positions are spaced exactly 256 kernel completions apart and do not align with any layer or operator boundary; the kernels bracketing each stall differ from stall to stall. During a stall the capture contains no host-side runtime call, no operator record and no device work of any kind, and the host thread is blocked inside the graph replay call for the whole step (source: `cpu_idle_metrics.json` -> `gpu_utilization.idle_time_percent`; `gpu_timeline.csv` -> `idle_time`; trace kernel and runtime event timestamps).

**Data:**

| Metric | Value | Flagged |
|--------|-------|---------|
| Idle time | 26080.5 ms (93.5%) | true |
| Idle in gaps >= 50 ms | 23096.6 ms (88.6% of idle) | true |
| Number of stalls >= 50 ms | 145 | true |
| Mean stall duration | 159.3 ms | true |
| Stall spacing inside a replay | every 256 kernel completions | true |
| Device busy time inside one replay | 38.7 ms of 835.5 ms | true |
| Communication time | 0.0 ms (0.0%) | false |
| MemCpy time | 1.8 ms (0.01%) | false |

**Reasoning for Slowdown:** A single decode step occupies 835 ms of wall time but contains only 38.7 ms of device work across 1176 kernels. Five stalls account for roughly 797 ms of the 806 ms of idle inside that step. The device therefore spends 95% of each step waiting rather than executing. The stall cadence is the decisive detail. A bottleneck rooted in the model would recur at layer boundaries and would change position when the kernel mix changes, whereas these stalls recur at a fixed completion count and hold that position across every replay in the capture. The same signature appears in the decode-only capture, where 160 stalls carry 97.1% of idle. The capture that executes without graph replay contains no stall of 50 ms or longer at all. Treating the 93.45% figure as a property of the workload would therefore misdirect tuning effort.

**Resolution:** Re-measuring with tracing reduced or disabled removes the per-completion bookkeeping that the stall cadence tracks, so the resulting timeline reflects dispatch behaviour instead of instrumentation behaviour. That gives a trustworthy baseline idle figure. Without that step, any subsequent optimisation would be scored against an idle number that the measurement itself produced, and real gains would be invisible underneath it.

**Impact estimate:** Impact estimate is not quantifiable from trace data.

<a id="detailed-analysis-system-p2"></a>
<!-- reasoning-candidate tier=system rank=2 -->
#### 🟡 P2: Host-paced dispatch leaves the device idle on the non-graph execution path

**Identification:** The capture that runs the mixed prefill-plus-decode shapes without graph replay was examined separately because it contains no long stalls and therefore isolates ordinary dispatch behaviour. In that capture the device is idle for 2928.9 ms of 3793.9 ms. 4050 gaps in the 100 us to 1 ms band carry 89.9% of that idle, with a median gap of 681 us between consecutive kernels. The same band accounts for 2359.9 ms in the mixed capture, which is the portion of its timeline that runs outside graph replay. By contrast, the gaps between kernels inside a replayed graph total about 9 ms per step across more than 1000 boundaries. Every category except kernel fusion is marked as carrying a host-side synchronisation bottleneck (source: `category_manifest.json` -> `categories[].has_sync_bottleneck`; trace kernel event timestamps for the prefill-decode and mixed captures).

**Data:**

| Metric | Value | Flagged |
|--------|-------|---------|
| Idle time on non-graph path | 2928.9 ms (77.2%) | true |
| Idle in 100 us - 1 ms gaps on that path | 2633.9 ms (89.9% of its idle) | true |
| Median inter-kernel gap, non-graph path | 0.681 ms | true |
| Count of 100 us - 1 ms gaps, non-graph path | 4050 | true |
| Idle in 100 us - 1 ms gaps, mixed capture | 2359.9 ms (9.0% of idle) | true |
| Idle inside a graph replay, per step | ~9 ms across ~1033 gaps | false |
| Categories flagged with host sync bottleneck | 6 of 7 | true |
| Total kernel launches in mixed capture | 38984 | true |

**Reasoning for Slowdown:** On the non-graph path the device waits about 681 us between kernels, which is longer than most of the kernels themselves. 78% of the 38984 launches in the mixed capture come from operations whose mean kernel time is under 10 us, and those launches together contribute only 172.5 ms of device work. The workload is therefore paced by how fast the host can issue work, not by how fast the device can complete it. The graph-replay path in the same run demonstrates the alternative: once the dispatch list is pre-recorded, the gaps between the same kind of kernels collapse to single-digit microseconds. The gap between the two paths in the same capture is direct evidence that per-operation host issue cost, not device capability, sets the pace.

**Resolution:** Replaying a pre-recorded dispatch list removes the per-operation host round trip that creates each 681 us gap, which is why the captured path already shows microsecond-scale gaps. Extending capture to the remaining shapes applies that same mechanism where it is currently absent. Fusion helps for the shapes that cannot be captured because it lowers the number of host issues required per step, and the launch count is what the idle time scales with on this path.

**Impact estimate:** Impact estimate is not quantifiable from trace data.

<a id="detailed-analysis-system-p3"></a>
<!-- reasoning-candidate tier=system rank=3 -->
#### 🟢 P3: Recurring small host-to-device stagings dominate the memory-copy event count

**Identification:** The memory-copy assessment was flagged because the host-to-device direction crosses the transfer-count threshold, not the time-share threshold. Seventy separate host-to-device transfers were recorded, well above the ten-transfer trigger, while their combined duration stays far below the five-percent time trigger. No device-to-host transfers appear at all, so there is no host read-back to investigate. (source: `multi_kernel_metrics.json` → `memcpy_assessment.flagged`, `memcpy_assessment.issues[].direction`, `memcpy_assessment.issues[].count`, `patterns_detected[].pattern`)

**Data:**

| Metric | Value | Flagged |
|--------|-------|---------|
| Total Memcpy Events | 398 (1.8 ms) | true |
| H2D Transfers | 70 (0.6 ms) | true |
| H2D Average Transfer Duration | 0.008 ms | true |
| H2D Maximum Transfer Duration | 0.009 ms | false |
| D2H Transfers | 0 (0.0 ms) | false |
| Unclassified-Direction Transfers | 328 (1.2 ms) | false |
| Exposed Memcpy Time | 1.8 ms (0.0%) | false |
| Exposed Communication Time | 0.0 ms (0.0%) | false |
| Total GPU Time | 27907.7 ms | false |

**Reasoning for Slowdown:** The memory-copy traffic is not a measurable source of slowdown in this trace. Exposed memory-copy time is 1.781 ms against a 27907.71 ms window, which is 0.01 percent of the total. The finding is a shape-of-traffic observation rather than a time cost. The signal worth noting is the repetition itself. Seventy host-to-device transfers clustered between 8.02 us and 9.42 us each is the signature of a fixed per-step payload that is re-staged rather than reused. Transfer byte counts are absent from this trace, so the payload size behind that repetition cannot be confirmed.

**Resolution:** Pinning the host buffer lets the copy engine issue a direct transfer instead of routing through a pageable-memory bounce buffer, which removes a host-side staging step from each of the seventy transfers. Hoisting step-invariant values into device-resident tensors removes the transfer entirely rather than making it faster, which is the larger win when the same payload is pushed every iteration. Issuing the remaining transfers on a dedicated copy stream lets them proceed concurrently with the compute stream instead of serializing against it. Because the absolute time involved is 1.781 ms, treat this as hygiene on the step path rather than a performance fix.

**Impact estimate:** Impact estimate is not quantifiable from trace data.
